Country X and Country Y operate a system where bankruptcy can be declared by the court upon the application of either the creditor or the debtor. Country X: If an individual cannot repay borrowed money, they may declare bankruptcy, and all assets they possess at the time of bankruptcy are distributed to the creditors. Any remaining debts are fully discharged. The court grants debt discharge except in cases where the debtor maliciously fails to pay despite having the ability to do so. A person who has been discharged through bankruptcy faces no restrictions on the freedoms and rights they enjoy as a citizen in daily life.Country Y: If an individual cannot repay borrowed money, they may declare bankruptcy, and all assets possessed at the time of bankruptcy are distributed to the creditors. However, unless the creditor agrees, debts to that creditor are not discharged. Creditors may exercise their rights without restriction over assets acquired by the debtor after bankruptcy until their full debt is repaid. The bankrupt individual is detained for a certain period, loses the right to vote until the debts are paid in full, and the bankruptcy record is made public. <question> Which of the following is NOT a correct analysis of the above passage? <choices> ① Someone who fears that individuals at risk of bankruptcy will keep taking on more debt to repay existing debt, thereby perpetuating creditor–debtor relationships, would oppose Country Y's system. ② Someone who believes that individuals are rational beings who make and are responsible for their own decisions, and that the state has no need to help those who have recklessly overspent, would oppose Country X's system. ③ Someone who is concerned that making creditor–debtor relationships after bankruptcy subject to the will of the creditor would cause social confusion, such as the emergence of fictitious creditors, would oppose Country Y's system. ④ Someone who worries that creditors may use bankruptcy filings as a means of threat in order to collect their claims ahead of other creditors would support Country Y's system. ⑤ Someone who is concerned that creditors will continue to urge bankrupt debtors to repay their debts and that related lawsuits will never cease would support Country X's system.

Alice is planning to speed on the highway today. There are no environmental factors that could frustrate this plan, and Alice’s determination is firm. In addition, once Alice makes up her mind, she never changes it. 'ⓐ Knowing all this, the police know that Alice will speed on the highway today.' In fact, Alice did speed on the highway. In this case, is it justified for the police to impose a speeding fine on Alice before she enters the highway? In other words, is it justified to punish someone in advance simply because it is known that they will commit an act that has not yet occurred? A: The significance of punishment is to inflict harm on a person equivalent to the wrongdoing they have committed, thus maintaining a balance. As long as it is known that a wrongdoing will be committed, the exact timing of the punishment is not important. It is the same principle as whether you pay for a TV before or after you receive it — it makes no difference. Regardless of whether the police impose the fine in advance, Alice will undoubtedly speed, and the police know this. Therefore, the police’s pre-emptive punishment to maintain balance in response to this can be justified.B: Punishing an innocent person cannot be justified under any circumstance. Even if Alice’s determination is strong, it cannot be denied that she has the ability to change her mind at the last moment and not speed. As long as Alice has that ability, before she actually speeds, she is clearly an innocent person. Therefore, pre-emptive punishment against Alice cannot be justified. <question> Which of the following analyses of the passage is/are correct? Choose all that apply from <statements>.<statements> (a). If ⓐ is false, the conclusion of A does not follow.(b). There is a view that, if the agent has the ability to decide whether or not to perform an act, it is impossible for others to know in advance whether she will perform that act. If this view is correct, B is incompatible with ⓐ.(c). A terrorist is preparing an attack that will drive citizens to their deaths, and the police know that if they leave this terrorist alone, the attack will succeed. The police respond by detaining the terrorist and meting out punishment in advance equivalent to the harm that would result from the attack, thereby successfully preventing it. According to A, pre-emptive punishment could be justified in this case as well. <choices> ① (c) ② (b), (c) ③ (a), (b), (c) ④ (a) ⑤ (a), (b)

<Theory> For an act to "cause harm" to someone means that, if the act had not occurred, that person would have been in a better state. Similarly, for an act to "benefit" someone means that, if the act had not occurred, that person would have been in a worse state. Alice and Bob have the following debate regarding <Theory>: Alice1: I could have given my friend 50,000 won for no reason but chose not to. If I had done so, my friend would have been in a better state. According to <Theory>, my act harmed my friend. But that seems unreasonable. Bob1: <Theory> doesn't have such implications. That's because doing nothing—like simply not giving your friend 50,000 won—cannot be considered an act. Alice2: If you limit "act" in such a way within <Theory>, other unreasonable consequences follow. Consider someone who saw a child struggling in water and had the ability to rescue them but chose not to, resulting in the child's drowning. Not saving the child clearly harmed the child. Bob2: But this case is different. The choice not to save the child is itself the result of a deliberate decision to avoid the rescue. In this sense, not saving the child should be considered an act. Alice3: Then what about this case? Imagine A bought a gift intended for B but became attached to it and decided to keep it instead of giving it to B. In this case, although not giving the gift was a deliberate decision, it doesn't seem like A harmed B. <question> Which of the following statements in <statements> is/are correct as an analysis of the above passage? <statements> (a) According to Alice1’s interpretation of <Theory>, if I could have punched my friend and broken their nose but did not do so, then, by not punching my friend, I performed an act that benefited my friend. (b) Alice2 and Bob2 differ in their judgment about whether not rescuing the child caused harm to the child. (c) If Bob, in response to Alice3, were to assert that “A’s not giving the gift to B did, in fact, harm B,” this would make Bob’s position inconsistent. <choices> ① (a) ② (a), (c) ③ (b) ④ (b), (c) ⑤ (a), (b), (c)

Alice: Elegance is not a property that belongs to Chopin's nocturnes themselves, but merely a subjective impression you have. When I listen to the nocturnes, I just feel bored the whole time. Bob: If you only felt boredom from listening to the nocturnes, that's because you're only used to hip-hop. Try to follow the delicacy expressed by the piano's tone and the development of the melody. The fact that this piece is elegant is something that anyone with an appropriate capacity for musical appreciation can recognize under normal conditions. Charlie: Even if the elegance of the nocturnes isn't just a matter of subjective feeling, I don't think it's correct to say it's a property that anyone can recognize. Isn't it rather that only people belonging to a certain culture, who are used to a particular kind of music, regard the nocturnes as elegant? This is at least unlike properties like the yellow color or round shape of a melon, which are genuinely attributable to the object itself. Bob: Even if only people from a certain group can regard the nocturnes as elegant, I think their elegance should still be seen as a genuine property of the music. After all, yellow is only seen as yellow by people who aren't color-blind, but it's still a real property of the melon, right? In the case of the nocturnes, it's just that only people with appropriate musical sensitivity can perceive the elegance. Charlie: Isn't it a more natural explanation that you two are reacting differently to the nocturnes because you each belong to groups that share different kinds of musical sensitivity? Alice: If I come to hold a belief based on insufficient evidence, that belief itself may not cause much harm. That belief could ultimately be true, and it might never be externally manifested in actions. However, I cannot avoid committing a crime against humanity by making myself an easy believer. The mere fact that a society holds false beliefs is a serious problem, but a greater problem is that society becomes gullible, loses the habit of examining and carefully investigating evidence, and regresses to a state of barbarism. 'ⓐ To believe something on insufficient evidence is always, everywhere, and for anyone, wrong.' - William Clifford, "The Ethics of Belief" - Bob: "Believe the truth!", "Avoid error!" These are the most important commandments for anyone seeking knowledge. However, these are two distinct rules. And depending on which of these one values more, one’s entire intellectual life may differ. One may prioritize the pursuit of truth and see the avoidance of error as secondary, or conversely, consider the avoidance of error most important and the attainment of truth as secondary. Clifford recommends the latter to us. He tells us that, rather than risking the dreadful possibility of believing a falsehood based on insufficient evidence, we should suspend judgment and believe nothing. As for myself, I don’t think I take Clifford’s side. In any case, what we must not forget is that our attitude toward the obligations related to truth or error is grounded not in evidence but in sentiment. People like Clifford, who say "It is better to never believe than to ever believe something false!" are merely expressing a fear of being naively deceived.- William James, "The Will to Believe" - <question> Which of the following analyses of the passages is/are correct? Choose as indicated from <statements>.<statements> (a) Alice supports her conclusion by pointing out the undesirable consequences that will arise if people do not act according to her conclusion. (b) According to Bob, Clifford's belief in ⓐ is not based on sufficient evidence. (c) Bob's argument requires the premise that 'even a belief based on sufficient evidence can be mistaken.' <choices> ① (a) ② (a), (b) ③ (c) ④ (a), (b), (c) ⑤ (b), (c)

In social sciences, classical experimental research may not be able to generalize experimental results to the real world. For example, suppose an experimental study was conducted to determine whether ‘watching a movie where a Black person appears as a hero’ (the experimental stimulus) reduces ‘the degree of negative prejudice against Black people’, and the following findings were observed. First, in the experimental group that received the experimental stimulus, the degree of prejudice was lower in the post-test than in the pre-test. Second, in the control group that did not receive the experimental stimulus, there was no change in the degree of prejudice between the pre-test and the post-test. In this case, it can be considered that watching the movie reduced the degree of prejudice among participants in the experimental group. However, it cannot be asserted with certainty that the same effect would appear if the movie was watched by people in their everyday lives. This is because in experiments, participants may already have become sensitive to the issue of prejudice against Black people as a result of the pre-test. To solve this problem, an <experimental design> that adds an experiment without a pre-test must be implemented. If, through this, experimental results are obtained that demonstrate ‘ⓐ that watching the movie reduced the degree of prejudice’, the possibility of generalization can be increased.<Experimental Design>• Group 1: Pre-test → Experimental stimulus → Post-test.• Group 2: Pre-test → Post-test.• Group 3: No pre-test → Experimental stimulus → Post-test.• Group 4: No pre-test → Post-test.All participants in Groups 1 to 4 were randomly selected from the population. <question> Which of the following cannot be included in the experimental results that demonstrate ⓐ? <choices> ① In Group 1, the degree of prejudice in the post-test was lower than the degree of prejudice in the pre-test. ② The degree of prejudice in the post-test of Group 3 was lower than the degree of prejudice in the post-test of Group 4. ③ The degree of prejudice in the post-test of Group 4 was lower than the degree of prejudice in the post-test of Group 1. ④ The degree of prejudice in the post-test of Group 1 was lower than the degree of prejudice in the post-test of Group 2. ⑤ The degree of prejudice in the post-test of Group 3 was lower than the degree of prejudice in the pre-test of Group 2.

The proposer is to suggest one of the following ways to split 10,000 won, which they will receive from the experimenter, with the responder:• 5-5 Option: The proposer and responder each get 5,000 won.• 8-2 Option: The proposer gets 8,000 won and the responder gets 2,000 won.• Coin Option: Toss a fair coin. If heads, the 5-5 option applies; if tails, the 8-2 option applies.The responder can accept or reject the proposer’s offer. If the responder accepts the proposed 5-5 or 8-2 option, the money is split as offered. <Theory> The concept of A consists of the characteristics that define A, that is, the characteristics that constitute the necessary and sufficient conditions for something to be A. For example, if the necessary and sufficient condition for an entity to be a “bachelor” is to be an unmarried man, then for an entity to be a bachelor, he must be both unmarried and male, and all entities who are both unmarried and male are bachelors. In this case, the concept of bachelor is composed of the characteristics of being unmarried and being male. If someone possesses the concept of A, they would use the concept of A to determine whether a specific entity belongs to category A or not. The time it takes to determine, using the concept of A, whether an entity falls under A is the sum of the time required to check whether that entity possesses each of the defining characteristics of A. <Experiment> Scientists presented participants with various kinds of animals, and asked them to perform a task to judge whether each animal was a bird. After posing questions like “Is x a bird?” they measured the time taken for participants to answer. The results showed that the average response time to say that a sparrow is a bird was 0.4 seconds, while for a penguin, it was 1.4 seconds on average. <question> Which of the following, as found among <statements>, is an appropriate evaluation of <Theory>? <statements> (a) If participants did not possess the concept of bird and answered based on the feel or impression of the words “sparrow” and “penguin,” then the results of <Experiment> do not weaken <Theory>. (b) If the time taken to confirm whether a sparrow and a penguin possess each characteristic that constitutes the concept of bird differs, then the results of <Experiment> weaken <Theory>. At the end of the 18th century, the French chemist Lavoisier argued that the combustion of a substance was a process in which the substance combined with another substance he named “oxygen.” However, this claim met with opposing arguments that it could not explain why heat was generated when a substance combined with oxygen. In response, he made the following assumptions: First, heat is actually a massless substance called “caloric,” and the generation of heat is a process by which caloric, which had been combined with a substance, is released. Second, gases contain far more caloric than solids or liquids. The reason why water turns into steam when an enormous amount of heat is supplied is because water and a large amount of caloric combine together. Similarly, gaseous oxygen is also a compound of oxygen and caloric. Based on these two assumptions, Lavoisier claimed that ‘ⓐ in the process of combustion, the oxygen in gaseous oxygen combines with the burning substance to form a compound, but the caloric in gaseous oxygen does not combine with the substance and escapes into the air, thus generating heat.’<question> Which of the following from <statements> are appropriate evaluations of ⓐ?<statements> (a) The fact that when many solid substances combust, heat is generated and gas is produced at the same time, strengthens ⓐ.(b) The fact that gunpowder, which contains compounds of oxygen, can combust explosively and release a massive amount of heat even without gaseous oxygen, weakens ⓐ.(c) The fact that, no matter how much heat generated during the combustion process is released into the air, the mass of air does not increase, weakens ⓐ. <choices> ① (a), (c) ② (b), (c) ③ (a), (b), (c) ④ (b) ⑤ (a)

Some people believe that in the not-so-distant future, if neuroscience is able to find the cause of all behavior within the brain, the practice of holding people legally responsible and punishing them will fundamentally change. Their view is that if a person’s criminal behavior is determined by causes in the brain, rather than stemming from free will, then it is not possible to hold that person responsible and punish them. However, this is a misconception arising from a misunderstanding of the law. The law assumes that people generally have the ability to make rational choices. There is general agreement that in order for someone to be exempt from legal responsibility, it must be proven that "the defendant lacks the capacity for rational action." The capacity for rational action here refers to the ability to act in ways that achieve one’s desires based on one’s own beliefs. Neuroscience may be able to help determine whether a person who committed a crime was rational at the time of the crime. However, unless neuroscience shows that people in general do not meet this minimum standard of rationality, it cannot justify a fundamental change in the way the law approaches responsibility. The law is not concerned with whether people possess metaphysical free will or not. The only concern of the law is whether people meet the minimum standard of rationality. <question> Which of the following statements in <statements> is correct as an evaluation of the above passage?<statements> (a) If neuroscience reveals that things like human beliefs or desires play no role in causing behavior, the argument of this passage would be weakened.(b) If neuroscience reveals that the very capacity for rational action in humans itself arises from the biological properties of brains evolved in a certain way, the argument of this passage would be weakened.(c) If neuroscience reveals that a large proportion of those who have committed crimes share common neural mechanisms that cause criminal behavior, the argument of this passage would be strengthened. <choices> ① (c) ② (a), (b), (c) ③ (a) ④ (a), (b) ⑤ (b), (c)

The Constitution is the highest law, establishing the fundamental values of the nation; if a statute violates the Constitution, that law becomes null and void. The question here is which aspect of a statute provides grounds for judging its unconstitutionality. One might say that the literal meaning of the legal text is the core aspect that serves as the basis for unconstitutionality, but in reality, while the Constitution prohibits discrimination, it is rare for a statute to explicitly contain words or sentences that say "discriminate." Fundamentally, the aspect of a law that is judged as unconstitutional is ⓐ ‘the direct consequence that is expected when the legal sentence representing the statute is applied to a specific case.’ For example, if Legal Sentence A contains content punishing those who commit adultery, the deciding aspect for the constitutionality of the law represented by A is the punishment imposed on those who commit adultery as a result of applying A. Some argue that we must examine ⓑ 'the impact that the enforcement of the statute has on the entire society.' For instance, in considering whether a statute giving extra points to a certain group in employment is unconstitutional due to discrimination, it is said that one must also observe the impact such granting of extra points has on others in the society. On the other hand, some still seek the decisive aspect for judgment of unconstitutionality in the meaning of the legal sentence, yet claim that the meaning of the legal sentence is ⓒ 'the contextual meaning that the legal sentence conveys within the context of the society’s history.' Whether a law represented by a legal sentence establishing a women-only educational institution violates the constitutional prohibition on discrimination depends on whether the establishment of such an institution aims to uplift women's status in the given country or is grounded in a historical context of separation and discrimination against women. <Situation> In Country X, after experiencing numerous wars, the national flag has become a symbol of the nation’s very existence, and flag burning is considered a criminal act that violates constitutional order, as it is regarded as an act undermining the authority of the state. However, when Country X’s parliament legislated Law L, represented by Legal Sentence R, to punish those who burn the national flag in order to protect the dignity and authority of the flag, acts of flag burning—which had almost never occurred previously—became frequent as opponents of the law protested, and sympathizers with the act of flag burning also grew in number. <question> From the following <statements>, which ones correctly evaluate the <situation>? <statements> (a) If ⓐ is considered the core aspect providing grounds for judgment of unconstitutionality, then Law L in Country X is unconstitutional.(b) The aspect ⓑ of Law L does not align with the legislative purpose of L as represented by R.(c) If ⓒ is considered the core aspect providing grounds for judgment of unconstitutionality, then Law L in Country X is unconstitutional. <choices> ① (a), (c) ② (a), (b), (c) ③ (b) ④ (b), (c) ⑤ (a)

Eighty years ago, Island K was unlawfully occupied by the state, resulting in the forced expulsion of the indigenous resident, Alice, from Island K, after which she struggled to live in a foreign land. If Alice were still alive, she should be compensated for the wrong committed by the state; however, Alice has already passed away. A debate arose as to whether compensation should now be made to Alice's surviving child, Bob. The following arguments were presented:Alice: Compensation should be given to the person affected by the wrongful act. ⓐ To compensate person S for wrongful act X is to provide S with benefits such that S achieves the standard of living that they would have enjoyed had X not occurred. Compensation should only occur when the victim’s standard of living has been worsened, and only in such cases. Therefore, compensation should be given to Bob to the extent that his standard of living would have been, had the unlawful occupation of Island K eighty years ago not occurred.Bob: There is a serious problem with Alice’s argument. Had the unlawful occupation of Island K not occurred, Bob’s father would not have met Bob’s mother, but instead would have met another woman, resulting in a completely different child being born—and Bob would not have existed at all. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that Bob would have enjoyed a higher standard of living if the unlawful occupation hadn’t happened; in fact, there is simply no answer to the question of what Bob’s standard of living would have been in that alternate scenario.Charlie: The wrongful act that gives rise to Bob's claim to compensation is not the unlawful occupation of Island K eighty years ago, but rather the fact that, at some point after Bob was born, no compensation was given to Alice for the occupation of Island K. If this had not been the case—in other words, if compensation had been given to Alice for the occupation after Bob was born—then Alice would have been able to provide Bob with better educational opportunities and resources, and Bob would have had a better life. Since such compensation was not given in the past, Bob must be compensated now. <question> Which of the following analyses of this debate are correct according to the <statements> below? <statements> (a) If Alice comes to accept that “Although Alice herself would have enjoyed a far higher standard of living than she actually did had the unlawful occupation of Island K not occurred eighty years ago, Bob would, on the contrary, have enjoyed a lower standard of living,” then she would not agree that compensation should be given to Bob.(b) If Bob accepts principle ⓐ, then he would agree that compensation should be made to Bob for the unlawful occupation of Island K eighty years ago.(c) Charlie does not agree with principle ⓐ, but agrees with Alice in that compensation should be made to Bob. <choices> ① (b), (c) ② (b) ③ (a), (b), (c) ④ (a), (c) ⑤ (a)
